title: Sampling, quantization, and aliasing
summary: Turn a continuous wave into samples and back on paper; say what quantization bits mean; explain why sampling creates aliases, list the aliases of any frequency, and derive the Nyquist limit Fₛ/2.
sourceNote: sampling_quantization.pdf, aliasing.pdf, Rosen & Howell (1991) ch. 14, Lab 2.

sections.heading: Why computers can't hold a wave

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The problem** A real sound wave is **continuous in time** (it has a value at every instant — infinitely many of them) and **continuous in amplitude** (any pressure, to infinite precision). A computer stores a finite list of finite-precision numbers. So two things have to be made discrete: *when* we look (sampling) and *how precisely* we record what we see (quantization). ==Everything in this chapter is the consequence of those two compromises== — including aliasing, the one that produces wrong answers silently.

blocks.body: **Sampling**: continuous time → a discrete sequence of time points, taken at regular intervals. **Quantization**: continuous amplitude → a discrete set of allowed amplitude levels.
the time between samples, in seconds.

blocks.md: - CD audio: Fₛ = 44,100 Hz. Speech corpora: often 16,000 Hz or 8,000 Hz (telephone).

blocks.title: Sampling cos(10πt) at two rates (the slides' example)

frames.caption: The signal. First rewrite 10π as 2π·5 so you can read the frequency: F = 5 Hz, period T = 0.2 s.
Sample at Fₛ = 10 Hz: a sample every 0.1 s. x[n] = cos(2π·5·n/10) = cos(πn) = 1, −1, 1, −1… Two samples per cycle. You can barely tell it's a cosine — it looks like a square wave.
Sample at Fₛ = 50 Hz: a sample every 0.02 s. x[n] = cos(2π·5·n/50) = cos(πn/5). Ten samples per cycle. Now it clearly traces the cosine. More samples per second = better approximation. (Lab 2 Q9.)

frames.note: samples in T seconds = T · Fₛ
frames.caption: The general formula. Sample n is taken at time n·Tₛ. Over T seconds you get T·Fₛ samples. Fₛ = 1/Tₛ.

blocks.title: Replace t with n/Fₛ. Everything else in the wave formula stays put.
blocks.body:
x[n] = x(n · Tₛ) = x(n / Fₛ)             n = 0, 1, 2, …
so for x(t) = A·cos(2πFt + ϕ):
x[n] = A·cos(2πF·n/Fₛ + ϕ)
number of samples in T seconds = T · Fₛ    (4 s at 100 Hz → 400 samples)
Lab 2: x[3] is taken at t = 3·Tₛ; with Tₛ = 0.005 s that's t = 0.015 s

**Lab 2 Q9 — the one that was marked wrong** 'How do we approximate x(t) better?' Only two things help: a **higher Fₛ** or, equivalently, a **shorter Tₛ** (same thing said twice). Changing the total duration T does nothing for the approximation — it just gives you more or fewer samples of the same quality. The four correct boxes were: higher Fₛ, shorter Tₛ; the T options were distractors.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** The sample-rate menu in every DAW — Audacity, Logic, Pro Tools — is exactly Fₛ, and the choices are this section's numbers: 44,100 Hz (CD), 48,000 Hz (video), 16,000 Hz (speech tech), 8,000 Hz (telephone). Zoom and phone calls sound 'thin' because they ship audio at the low rates: an 8 kHz stream simply has no room for anything above 4 kHz (the aliasing section explains why exactly half). And Whisper, like nearly every modern speech recognizer, resamples whatever you give it to 16 kHz before doing anything else — ==x[n] = x(n/Fₛ) is the first line of every speech pipeline==.

Choose a set of allowed amplitude levels and snap every sample to one of them — in Koo's convention, snap *down*: ==take the highest level that doesn't exceed the value==. The number of levels is the **resolution**. Levels are indexed by integers and stored in bits, so the count is a power of 2: **3 bits → 2³ = 8 levels (0–7); 5 bits → 32; 8 bits → 256; 16 bits → 65,536** (CD quality). More bits = finer steps = less rounding error (**quantization noise**).

The smooth wave (green) can take any value; the stored signal (blue staircase) must sit on one of 2³ = 8 levels, snapping down to the highest level that doesn't exceed each sample. The red gap is quantization error — the noise that more bits shrink. At CD quality (16 bits) there are 65,536 levels, so the staircase hugs the wave far too closely to hear. Hover any part.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Bit depth is the other number on every recording device: CDs are 16-bit, studio interfaces record at 24-bit, and old game consoles were 8-bit — the crunchy sound of a 'bit-crusher' plugin is literally this staircase made coarse on purpose. Each extra bit halves the step size, which works out to ##about 6 dB less quantization noise per bit## — that's why spec sheets say '16-bit ≈ 96 dB dynamic range', and it's the same 20·log₁₀(2) ≈ 6 dB you computed in Chapter 0.

sections.heading: Aliasing: two waves that look the same after sampling

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why it exists** In old westerns, wagon wheels seem to spin backward. The camera takes 24 pictures a second; if a spoke rotates *almost* a full turn between frames, the eye reads it as barely moving backward. Sampling a sound does the same thing: a high frequency, sampled too slowly, produces exactly the same list of numbers as some lower frequency. Those two frequencies are **aliases** of each other, and !!once you've sampled, no algorithm can ever tell them apart!! — the information is gone, not hidden.

The samples land exactly where a slow 1 Hz cosine (red, dashed) would put them: cos(2π·7·n/8) = cos(2π·1·n/8) for every n. The computer keeps only the dots, so it reconstructs the red wave, not the green one — the wagon wheel spinning backward, in audio. Hover any part.
blocks.slide: Two waves, one set of samples

blocks.title: The proof, one line at a time
blocks.body:
Show that cos(2πFt) and cos(2π(F + Fₛ)t) give identical samples at rate Fₛ.

1. Samples are taken at t = n/Fₛ. So the samples of the second wave are cos(2π(F + Fₛ)·n/Fₛ).
2. Distribute: cos(2πF·n/Fₛ + 2πFₛ·n/Fₛ) = cos(2πF·n/Fₛ + 2πn).
3. 2πn is a whole number of full turns. Cosine is 2π-periodic, so cos(x + 2πn) = cos(x).
4. Therefore = cos(2πF·n/Fₛ) — exactly the samples of the first wave. Adding Fₛ to the frequency changes nothing after sampling.
blocks.slide: Why F and F + Fₛ are aliases (the slides' algebra)

blocks.body: because cosine is even, cos(2π·F·t) = cos(2π·(−F)·t). A negative frequency is just the point going around the circle the other way; its shadow is identical.
for any integer k: adding or subtracting whole multiples of the sampling rate (the proof above).

blocks.md: - So the aliases of F sampled at Fₛ are: …, −F − Fₛ, −F, −F + Fₛ, F, F + Fₛ, F + 2Fₛ, … and −F + 2Fₛ, etc.
blocks.slide: All the aliases of F (aliasing.pdf slide 5)

blocks.title: Fₛ = 1000 Hz, frequencies 0 to 1000
blocks.body:
Find the alias pairs and the pattern.

1. Aliases of F include −F + Fₛ = 1000 − F. So 100 Hz pairs with 900, 200 with 800, 300 with 700, 400 with 600, and 0 with 1000.
2. Pattern (Q13, Q15): **F₂ = Fₛ − F₁**. The pairs are mirror images around Fₛ/2 = 500 Hz.
3. 500 Hz pairs with itself. That's the edge — the Nyquist frequency (Q11, Q14).
blocks.answer: F₂ = Fₛ − F₁; Nyquist = Fₛ/2 = 500 Hz

blocks.title: Why Fₛ/2 is the limit
blocks.body:
We want a range 0 to F_max with no aliases inside it. How high can F_max be?

1. F must be below Fₛ, because 0 and Fₛ are aliases — if the range reached Fₛ, the very first alias would be inside it.
2. Among the aliases of a frequency F, the one that could fall below Fₛ is −F + Fₛ. It must not land inside the range, i.e. it must not be below F.
3. Require −F + Fₛ ≥ F. Rearrange: Fₛ ≥ 2F, so **F ≤ Fₛ/2**.
4. So the alias-free range is 0 to Fₛ/2. That upper limit is the **Nyquist frequency**. To represent frequencies up to F, sample at least at 2F.

blocks.caption: With Fₛ = 1000 Hz: every frequency above 500 folds back onto its mirror image below 500 (F₂ = Fₛ − F₁, the Lab 2 Q15 pattern). 900 Hz is indistinguishable from 100 Hz after sampling. Hover any part.

blocks.body: Sampling at Fₛ makes F indistinguishable from −F and from F ± kFₛ (and −F ± kFₛ). The alias-free band is 0 to **Fₛ/2**, the Nyquist frequency. To capture frequencies up to F, sample at Fₛ ≥ 2F. (Speech at 16 kHz captures up to 8 kHz; telephone 8 kHz captures up to 4 kHz — which is why phones sound dull.)

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Aliasing lives everywhere a camera or an ADC does: the wagon-wheel effect in film, helicopter rotors that hang frozen on video, and the moiré ripples when someone wears a striped shirt on camera — the stripes beat against the sensor's pixel grid, which is spatial aliasing. It's why every microphone chip puts an **anti-aliasing filter** in front of the sampler to physically remove everything above Fₛ/2 — !!aliasing cannot be undone in software afterward!!, so it must be prevented in hardware before. And it's why CDs run at 44.1 kHz: hearing tops out near 20 kHz, Nyquist demands at least 40 kHz, and the extra 4.1 kHz gives the filter room to roll off.

blocks.prompt: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. What frequency will it appear to be?
blocks.answer: Its alias −7 + 10 = 3 kHz. It folds back to 3 kHz (mirror of 7 around Nyquist = 5).

blocks.prompt: Lab 2 Q14: what's the Nyquist frequency in terms of Fₛ, and why does the answer 'Fₛ − F' appear as a choice?
blocks.answer: Nyquist = Fₛ/2. 'Fₛ − F' is the *alias* of F, not the Nyquist frequency — it's the Q15 answer (F₂ = Fₛ − F₁), planted as a distractor in Q14.

exercises.title: Samples, intervals, and what x[n] is
exercises.prompt: x(t) = cos(2π·50·t), sampled at Fₛ = 400 Hz for 0.1 s. (a) Tₛ? (b) how many samples? (c) write x[n] as a formula in n; (d) what is x[4]? (e) how many samples per cycle of the cosine?
hints: Tₛ = 1/Fₛ. Number of samples = duration × Fₛ. Substitute t = n/Fₛ into x(t) for the formula.
People compute x[4] at t = 4 seconds. Sample 4 is at t = 4·Tₛ = 4/400 = 0.01 s.
Samples per cycle = Fₛ / F. If that number is small (near 2) the samples barely trace the wave — Lab 2 Q9.
solution: (d) x[4] = cos(π) = −1 — that's t = 0.01 s, half a period of the 50 Hz wave. ✓
exercises.why: Every recording you ever process is x[n], not x(t). Knowing which second a sample index corresponds to — and how many samples one cycle of a pitch takes — is the arithmetic behind pitch trackers, speech recognizers, and every 'why does my plot look wrong' moment in Colab.

exercises.title: Find the alias
exercises.prompt: A microphone samples at Fₛ = 8000 Hz (telephone quality). (a) What's the Nyquist frequency? (b) A 5000 Hz whistle gets in. What frequency will it appear as after sampling? (c) A 9000 Hz tone? (d) Explain in one sentence why phone calls sound dull.

choices.text: (b) It appears as 5000 Hz — sampling doesn't change frequency
choices.feedback: It does when F is above Fₛ/2. 5000 is above 4000, so it folds. Compute Fₛ − F.
Right. −5000 + 8000 = 3000 Hz — the mirror image of 5000 around Nyquist (4000).
That's 5000 − 4000, the distance *above* Nyquist, not the folded frequency. Fold it: Fₛ − F = 3000.

hints: Nyquist = Fₛ/2. Anything above it folds back. The aliases of F are ±F ± k·Fₛ; find the one that lands in 0..Fₛ/2.
The usual mistake is subtracting from Nyquist instead of from Fₛ. Mirror around Nyquist means F₂ = Fₛ − F₁ (Lab 2 Q15), which is the same as −F + Fₛ.
For 9000 Hz, subtract a whole Fₛ first: 9000 − 8000 = 1000. That's already below Nyquist.
solution: (c) 9000 − 8000 = 1000 Hz (an alias of 9000 in the base band).

(d) Sampling at 8 kHz can only represent frequencies up to 4 kHz, and consonants like /s/ live above that — so the phone throws them away (and must filter them out first, or they'd alias into the speech band as garbage).
exercises.why: Anti-aliasing filters exist in every ADC because of this arithmetic. If you ever record data — audio, sensor readings, video frames of a spinning wheel — 'is my sample rate at least twice the highest frequency present?' is the first question, and getting it wrong produces errors that look like real signal.
